# How the proof works: Kourovka 21.40

**Agent-generated exposition; not refereed.** This informal account was generated by **Nilradical v0** after [human acceptance](../nilradical-v0-acceptance/README.md) of the linked proof snapshot. It has not been refereed and may simplify details. The exact mathematical claims are the linked Lean statements and proofs; acceptance of that snapshot does not imply human review of this prose.

## The statement and its strengthening

Problem 21.40, attributed to A. Dantas and E. de Melo, asks whether a subgroup $G$ of $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb{Q})$ with finitely many orbits under its automorphism group must be virtually soluble. The accepted answer is stronger. There is a normal finite-index subgroup $K$, torsion-free and nilpotent of class at most $n-1$, with

$$
[G : K] \le (2n+1)^{n^2}.
$$

One rational change of basis makes every element of $K$ upper unitriangular. No finite-generation hypothesis is needed. The solution, quantitative strengthening, number-field extension, and Lean formalization are credited to **Nilradical v0** in the [accepted overview](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/README.md).

The formal hypothesis [`HasFiniteAutomorphismOrbits`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Statement.lean#L20) uses the full abstract automorphism group acting on $G$ by evaluation. Automorphisms need not come from ambient matrix conjugation. [`StructuralConclusion`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Statement.lean#L42) separately requires actual finite index and its numerical bound. This distinction matters because the natural-number index convention assigns zero to infinite index. Likewise, nilpotence is explicitly asserted before its class bound. Dimension zero is included: $\operatorname{GL}_0(\mathbb{Q})$ is trivial, and natural subtraction interprets $n-1$ as zero there.

The argument connects three kinds of information: finitely many automorphism orbits produce arbitrarily deep roots; arithmetic turns those roots into finitely many possible traces; finite-dimensional algebra turns finite traces into a unitriangular subgroup of finite index. The last step follows the classical finite-trace tradition associated with Burnside, Procesi, and Kolchin, discussed in Kaplansky's *Fields and Rings*. Earlier work of Bastos, Dantas, and de Melo treated related structure under additional hypotheses such as solubility, finite rank, or virtual nilpotence; the references are retained in the accepted overview.

## From automorphism orbits to roots of unity

Start with a sufficiently large prime $p$. On the units of any fixed finite-dimensional rational algebra, taking the $p$th power is injective. A cyclotomic argument proves this even when the algebra is noncommutative. The polynomial $\Phi_p$ has degree $p-1$, larger than the relevant minimal-polynomial degree, so it is coprime to that minimal polynomial. Applied to a linear map, this shows that a vector fixed by its $p$th power was already fixed by the map. Applied to conjugation by a unit $u$, it says that commuting with $u^p$ forces commuting with $u$.

If $u^p = v^p$, this fixed-vector result makes $u$ and $v$ commute. Their quotient then has $p$th power one, and another use of the cyclotomic argument makes that quotient trivial. [`exists_prime_pow_injective`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/MatrixRoots.lean#L158) packages the matrix version. The proof chooses a coarse dimension-dependent prime; its numerical size is irrelevant to the public index bound.

Powering commutes with every abstract automorphism. Its injectivity on $G$ therefore induces an injective map on the finite orbit set, which must be surjective. Surjectivity on orbit classes lifts to surjectivity on elements by applying an appropriate automorphism to a chosen root. This general bridge is [`surjective_pow_of_injective`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/Orbits.lean#L44). Repeatedly choosing roots gives a coherent chain $b_0 = g$ and $b_{k+1}^p = b_k$, formalized by [`exists_root_chain`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/Orbits.lean#L53).

The arithmetic step needs all the relevant scalar roots in a single number field. The subalgebras $\mathbb{Q}[b_k]$ form an increasing chain because each earlier matrix is a power of the next. Finite dimensionality forces stabilization, as recorded in [`exists_stable_adjoin_of_root_chain`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/Eigenvalues.lean#L17). After stabilization, every root matrix is a polynomial in one matrix. Polynomial relations can then be evaluated at a complex spectral value of that matrix, transferring the deep-root equations to the number field generated by that scalar. Spectral mapping relates these values back to the eigenvalues of $g$.

Northcott finiteness now forces each such nonzero scalar to be a root of unity. Indeed, the logarithmic heights of roots $y$ satisfying $y^{p^k} = z$ are bounded by the height of $z$. A fixed number field contains only finitely many elements with that height bound. Two roots at different depths must coincide; the two power equations then give a positive power equal to one. [`exists_pow_eq_one_of_deep_roots`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/DeepRoots.lean#L16) uses mathlib's number-field height development for this argument.

Every eigenvalue of $g$ is consequently a root of unity. Its trace is a sum of algebraic integers, and also rational, so it is an integer. Each eigenvalue has complex absolute value one, yielding $-n \le \operatorname{tr}(g) \le n$. The assembled theorem is [`trace_bounds_of_finite_automorphism_orbits`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/FiniteOrbits.lean#L17). This is a restriction on traces and eigenvalues; it does not assert that every matrix in $G$ has finite order, since nontrivial unipotent matrices may remain.

## From finitely many traces to a finite-index subgroup

Now let $A$ be the rational matrix algebra spanned by $G$. Define its trace ideal $I$ to consist of $r \in A$ satisfying $\operatorname{tr}(rb) = 0$ for every $b \in A$. Cyclic invariance of trace makes $I$ a two-sided ideal. Every positive power of $r \in I$ has zero trace. Newton–Girard identities identify its characteristic polynomial with that of the zero matrix, and Cayley–Hamilton gives $r^n = 0$. Thus every element of $I$ is nilpotent. The Newton–Girard component adapts the TNLean contributors' code in LionSR/QICLean; its exact provenance and Apache license are retained in [THIRD_PARTY.md](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/THIRD_PARTY.md).

The subgroup [`traceKernel`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/TraceKernel.lean#L79) is $K = \{g \in G : g-1 \in I\}$; the ideal identities make it normal. Choose a basis $b_1,\ldots,b_d$ of $A$ from matrices in $G$, where $d \le n^2$. Associate to $g$ its trace vector $(\operatorname{tr}(gb_1),\ldots,\operatorname{tr}(gb_d))$. Each coordinate is an integer in $[-n,n]$, because $gb_i$ belongs to $G$. Two trace vectors are equal exactly when the elements lie in the same coset of $K$: equality on the basis extends linearly to the defining trace equations for $I$. There are at most $(2n+1)^d$ possible vectors, proving actual finiteness of the quotient and the claimed bound.

## One common unitriangular basis

A common basis is still required: individual nilpotence does not itself supply simultaneous triangularity. The proof shows that a nil left ideal annihilates every simple module. Otherwise simplicity would produce an element of the ideal fixing a nonzero vector, contradicting its nilpotence. Induction through a finite-length module builds a rational basis in which $I$ acts strictly upper triangularly. [`exists_conjugating_strict_upper`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Proof/RationalFlag.lean#L148) packages that basis as one matrix $P$. Since $g-1 \in I$ for every $g \in K$, this same $P$ makes all of $K$ upper unitriangular.

The superdiagonal commutator filtration gives class at most $n-1$. This component adapts the Tau Ceti contributors' proof, with provenance in the same third-party record. Over $\mathbb{Q}$, a finite-order unipotent matrix is the identity; the formal proof uses the squarefree annihilator of a finite-order operator together with nilpotence of its difference from the identity. Conjugation transfers both conclusions to $K$. [`structural_theorem`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Solution.lean#L20) assembles these branches, and virtual solubility follows from nilpotence.

## Number fields and the accepted scope

For a number field $F$, restriction of scalars faithfully represents $G$ on a finite-dimensional rational vector space. The full abstract automorphism-orbit condition is preserved by the resulting group isomorphism. Applying the rational theorem and transporting its subgroup back proves [`numberField_structure`](https://github.com/alunik/kourovka-lean/blob/5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5/Kourovka/Problems/P21_40/Solution.lean#L72): a finite-index torsion-free nilpotent subgroup exists. This public extension does not assert the rational dimension-only bound or a simultaneous conjugator over $F$ in the original dimension.

## Reading and verification

No search or external computational certificate supplies any premise here. The finite counts, polynomial identities, and arithmetic arguments are proved symbolically. For a reading route, start with the statement and structural assembly, then follow the root-to-trace branch and the trace-ideal-to-flag branch. An ordinary build uses `LEAN_NUM_THREADS=1 lake build Kourovka.Problems.P21_40.Solution`. The [verification record](../nilradical-v0-verification/README.md) gives the stronger procedure: fresh compilation, independently reviewed statement comparison, and Lean plus Nanoda replay under the three-axiom policy. The [statement audit](../nilradical-v0-verification/statement-audits/21.40.md) and subsequent human decision address mathematical interpretation separately. Every source link here pins accepted revision `5a6b2c18e326b7b0281f00b64cade629acbfe1f5`; improving the bounds or extending the field hypotheses remains further work.
